entry: American actress. She made her feature film debut in *A Nightmare on Elm Street 3: Dream Warriors* (1987). She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for the coming-of-age film *Boyhood* (2014), which was filmed from 2002 until 2014. On television she won a Primetime Emmy Award for the supernatural drama *Medium* in 2005, and another for *The Act* (2019). She has starred in the Apple TV thriller *Severance* since 2022.

American actress. She won Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Comedy Series in 2000 and 2001 for playing Debra Barone in the CBS sitcom *Everybody Loves Raymond* (1996–2005). From 2009 to 2018 she starred as Frankie Heck in the ABC comedy *The Middle*. She also hosted and produced the Food Network series *Patricia Heaton Parties* (2015–16), which won a Daytime Emmy Award.

American novelist and short story writer known for [[Thriller (genre)|psychological thrillers]], including five novels about the character Tom Ripley. Her breakthrough novel, *Strangers on a Train* (1950), was adapted into a 1951 film directed by [[Alfred Hitchcock]]. *The Talented Mr. Ripley* (1955) cemented her reputation as a leading suspense novelist. Her novel *The Price of Salt* (1952), published under a pseudonym, was groundbreaking for its positive depiction of lesbian relationships. She moved to Switzerland in 1982.

American stage and film actress. She won the Academy Award for Best Actress for *Hud* (1963) and the 1947 Tony Award for Best Featured Actress in a Play for *Another Part of the Forest*. Her other films include *The Day the Earth Stood Still* (1951), *A Face in the Crowd* (1957) and *Breakfast at Tiffany's* (1961). After three strokes in 1965 she relearned to walk and talk, and she later established a stroke rehabilitation center in [[Knoxville, Tennessee|Knoxville]].

American football quarterback for the Kansas City Chiefs of the [[National Football League|NFL]]. He became the Chiefs' starter in 2018 and was named NFL Most Valuable Player that season. He won three [[Super Bowl]] championships, LIV, LVII and LVIII, and was named Super Bowl Most Valuable Player in each. In 2020 he signed a 10-year contract extension worth over $450 million. He was also named NFL Most Valuable Player in 2022.

English actor, a member of the Royal Shakespeare Company from 1966. He won three Laurence Olivier Awards, two of them for Best Actor in a Supporting Role, and was knighted in 2010 for services to drama. He played Captain Jean-Luc Picard in *Star Trek: The Next Generation* and in its films, and Professor Charles Xavier in the *X-Men* film series. He reprised Xavier in the [[Marvel Cinematic Universe]].

American actor, singer-songwriter and dancer, known for romantic, tough and comic roles. He received Golden Globe nominations for *Dirty Dancing* (1987), *Ghost* (1990) and *To Wong Foo, Thanks for Everything! Julie Newmar* (1995). He also starred in *Road House* (1989) and *Point Break* (1991). He co-wrote "She's Like the Wind", which peaked at number three on the Billboard Hot 100. He received a star on the [[Hollywood Walk of Fame]] in 1997 and died of [[Pancreatic cancer|pancreatic cancer]].

Feeling of love, devotion and attachment to one's country or state. It may combine attachment to a homeland's language, ethnicity, culture, politics and history, and it is closely related to civic [[Nationalism|nationalism]]. In the 19th century patriotism and nationalism had similar meanings, but nationalism has since taken on negative connotations. [[George Orwell]] contrasted the two in *Notes on Nationalism*, describing patriotism as defensive and nationalism as inseparable from the desire for power. Among Enlightenment thinkers, [[Jean-Jacques Rousseau]] was an influential proponent of patriotism, while [[Samuel Johnson]] wrote in 1774 that patriotism is "the last refuge of the scoundrel." Johnson's remark is usually read as an attack on patriotism itself, though some argue he targeted false patriotism. Many patriotic people take pride in a distinct common culture and encourage [[Cultural assimilation|cultural assimilation]] by others, while civic forms of patriotism tend to de-emphasize ethnic culture.

American country singer, one of the first country artists to cross over into [[Pop music|pop]] music. Her first major hit, "Walkin' After Midnight" (1957), reached both the country and pop charts. After moving to [[Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]] in 1958, she had hits including "I Fall to Pieces" (1961), her first to top the Billboard country chart, and "Crazy." She was the first female performer inducted into the Country Music Hall of Fame, in 1973. She was killed in a plane crash.

American singer, songwriter and poet, nicknamed the "Godmother of Punk." Her debut album, *Horses* (1975), made her an influential figure in the New York City [[Punk rock|punk rock]] movement, and she has fused rock and poetry in her work. Her song "Because the Night," co-written with [[Bruce Springsteen]], reached number 13 on the Billboard Hot 100 chart. Her memoir *Just Kids* won the National Book Award in 2010. She was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] in 2007.

American actress who played [[Helen Keller]] in *The Miracle Worker* (1962), winning the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress at age 15. She starred as the identical cousins Cathy and Patty Lane in *The Patty Duke Show* (1963–1966) and won a Golden Globe for her performance in *Me, Natalie* (1969). She served as president of the Screen Actors Guild from 1985 to 1988. After she was diagnosed with [[Bipolar disorder|bipolar disorder]] in 1982, she became a public advocate for mental health education.

American actress and member of the Hearst family, granddaughter of [[William Randolph Hearst]]. She was [[Kidnapping|kidnapped]] in 1974 by the Symbionese Liberation Army (SLA) and was arrested 19 months later as a fugitive. She testified that she had been raped and threatened while held captive. The prosecution argued that she had joined the group voluntarily. In 1976 she was convicted of bank robbery and sentenced to 35 years in prison, later reduced to seven years. [[Jimmy Carter]] commuted her sentence, and [[Bill Clinton]] later pardoned her. In the 1990s she began acting after [[John Waters]] approached her.

American businessman and philanthropist who co-founded [[Microsoft]] with [[Bill Gates]] in 1975. He owned the Seattle Seahawks of the [[National Football League]] and the Portland Trail Blazers of the [[National Basketball Association]]. Through Vulcan Inc., founded in 1986 to manage his business and philanthropy, he gave more than $2 billion to causes including education, conservation and the arts. He funded SpaceShipOne, the first crewed private spaceplane. He also discovered the wrecks of the Japanese battleship *Musashi* and USS *Indianapolis*.

Canadian-born singer, songwriter and actor. His song "Diana" went to number one on the Canadian and U.S. charts. He wrote the English lyrics to "My Way," [[Frank Sinatra]]'s signature song, and the theme for *The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson*. He wrote "She's a Lady" for [[Tom Jones (singer)|Tom Jones]] and toured Britain and Australia with [[Buddy Holly]]. He co-wrote three songs with [[Michael Jackson]], which became posthumous hits for Jackson.

Cameroonian politician, president of [[Cameroon]] since 1982. He was prime minister under Ahmadou Ahidjo from 1975 until Ahidjo resigned in 1982, and then succeeded him as president. He consolidated power after an attempted coup in 1984. He introduced political reforms within a one-party system in the 1980s and accepted multiparty politics in the early 1990s under pressure. His Cameroon People's Democratic Movement rules as a de facto one-party state. Biya has been re-elected by large margins in 1997, 2004, 2011, 2018 and 2025, and opposition politicians and Western governments have alleged voting irregularities and fraud in these elections. He is widely described as a dictator. He is the second-longest-ruling president in Africa, after Teodoro Obiang Nguema Mbasogo of [[Equatorial Guinea]].

French Post-Impressionist painter who formed the bridge between [[Impressionism]] and [[Cubism]]. His early work was influenced by Romanticism and Realism, but he developed a new pictorial language by studying Impressionist forms. He altered conventional approaches to perspective, emphasizing the underlying structure of objects, and built up forms from planes of color and small, exploratory brushstrokes. His paintings initially provoked ridicule. Until the late 1890s his champions were mainly fellow artists such as [[Camille Pissarro]] and the dealer Ambroise Vollard, who gave him a first solo exhibition in Paris in 1895. [[Henri Matisse]] and [[Pablo Picasso]] are said to have remarked that Cézanne "is the father of us all."

English theoretical physicist and a founder of [[Quantum mechanics|quantum mechanics]]. In 1928 he formulated the [[Dirac equation]], which combined [[Special relativity|special relativity]] with quantum mechanics and predicted the existence of [[Antimatter|antimatter]]. He shared the 1933 Nobel Prize in Physics with [[Erwin Schrödinger]] for new productive forms of atomic theory. He laid foundations for [[Quantum electrodynamics|quantum electrodynamics]] and quantum field theory, and contributed to Fermi–Dirac statistics, which describes fermions. He was Lucasian Professor of Mathematics at the [[University of Cambridge|University of Cambridge]] from 1932 to 1969, and a professor at Florida State University from 1970 to 1984. His 1930 monograph *The Principles of Quantum Mechanics* is among the most influential texts on the subject.

French painter, sculptor and printmaker associated with Post-Impressionism and Symbolism. A stockbroker until the financial crisis of 1882, he took up painting full-time, mentored by [[Camille Pissarro]], and exhibited with the [[Impressionism|Impressionists]] in the early 1880s. His work in [[Brittany]] and [[Martinique]] depicted native life and landscapes. He then settled in [[Tahiti]], then a French colony, seeking refuge from Western civilization, and his paintings there used vivid color and Symbolist themes. Ill health and financial struggles marked his later years in Tahiti and the Marquesas Islands. His reputation grew after his death, partly through the efforts of dealer Ambroise Vollard, and he influenced [[Pablo Picasso]], [[Henri Matisse]] and the French avant-garde.

Rwandan politician and former military officer, president of [[Rwanda]] since 2000. He commanded the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), a rebel force that ended the [[Rwandan genocide|1994 genocide]]. He was vice president and defense minister from 1994 to 2000 and the country's de facto leader. Kagame sponsored two rebel wars in Zaire. The first, backed by Rwanda and Uganda, installed Laurent-Désiré Kabila as president and renamed the country the [[Democratic Republic of the Congo]]. The second lasted until a 2003 peace deal. Under Kagame, Rwanda has pursued national development, with gains in healthcare, education and economic growth. Human rights groups accuse his government of political repression, and none of his four presidential elections has been rated free or fair by international observers. Kagame denies allegations that Rwanda supports insurgents in the DRC.

Swiss-born German painter and draftsman whose style was influenced by [[Expressionism|expressionism]], [[Cubism|cubism]] and [[Surrealism|surrealism]]. He explored [[Color theory|color theory]] extensively, and his lectures, published in English as the *Paul Klee Notebooks*, are held to be as important for modern art as [[Leonardo da Vinci]]'s *A Treatise on Painting* was for the Renaissance. He taught at the [[Bauhaus]] alongside [[Wassily Kandinsky]]. Klee first trained as a violinist and chose the visual arts as a teenager. The Nazi regime branded his art degenerate and barred him from exhibiting after 1933, and he settled permanently in Switzerland, where scleroderma progressively impaired his health.

American comedian, actor and game-show panelist known for a campy, snarky persona. He played Uncle Arthur on [[Bewitched]] and the father Harry MacAfee in *Bye Bye Birdie* on Broadway. He was a regular "center square" panelist on *The Hollywood Squares* and voiced characters in five [[Hanna-Barbera]] productions. Mel Brooks said Lynde could get laughs by reading "a phone book, tornado alert, or seed catalog."

English singer, songwriter and bassist, best known as a member of [[The Beatles]]. He shared songwriting and lead vocal duties with [[John Lennon]], and their partnership remains the most successful in music history. Many of his Beatles songs, including "Yesterday," "Eleanor Rigby" and "Blackbird," are among the most covered in history. After the Beatles broke up he released the solo album *McCartney* (1970) and formed the band Wings, which had many hits in the 1970s. His estimated sales total 100 million records, and he has won 19 [[Grammy Awards]]. He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] twice, as a Beatle and as a solo artist.

American actor, filmmaker and race car driver. He won the Academy Award for Best Actor for *The Color of Money* (1986), after earlier Oscar-nominated performances in *Cat on a Hot Tin Roof*, *The Hustler* and *Hud*. He won several Sports Car Club of America national championships as a driver. He co-founded Newman's Own, a food company that donates all its post-tax profits and royalties to charity and has donated over US$600 million. He was married to actress [[Joanne Woodward]], with whom he often worked on screen.

American actor and comedian who created and played the character Pee-wee Herman. Pee-wee debuted in a 1981 stage show. The film *Pee-wee's Big Adventure* (1985), directed by [[Tim Burton]], was a success. Reubens then starred as Pee-wee on the [[CBS]] children's series *Pee-wee's Playhouse* (1986–1990), which won 15 Emmy Awards. He was arrested for indecent exposure in 1991, which significantly harmed his career. In 2002 he was charged with child pornography offenses, which he denied; he later pleaded guilty to a misdemeanor obscenity charge under a plea deal. He revived Pee-wee on stage in the 2010s.

American silversmith, military officer and industrialist. A supporter of the Patriot cause in [[Boston]], he made a midnight ride in 1775 to alert minutemen to approaching British troops before the [[Battles of Lexington and Concord]]. His ride was dramatized in [[Henry Wadsworth Longfellow]]'s poem "Paul Revere's Ride," which made him an American folk hero. His militia service ended after the Penobscot Expedition, one of the most disastrous American campaigns of the war, though he was absolved of blame. He returned to silversmithing and became the first American to roll copper into sheets for sheathing naval vessels.
